extracted.intended_audience: judges, lawyers, law students, and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on evidentiary standards, the sufficiency of specifications (enablement), identity/infringement, novelty, utility, and the respective roles of court, jury, and expert witnesses in patent trials. Explains how to construe specifications and claims in light of the state of the art and the inventor's actual contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of the specification (enablement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must enable the public to do what the inventor says he has enabled them to do by his specification and plan; omission of essential dimensions or directions (e.g., centre of eccentric, crank position) that can only be ascertained by subsequent experiments renders the specification bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat drawings as illustrations not as binding dimensions; determine sufficiency by whether a workman of ordinary and competent skill and knowledge could construct the invention without exercising inventive faculty. Evidence from witnesses who say they could construct from the specification is relevant, but the proper test is what a person of ordinary skill could do.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings are illustrative, not limiting
rubrics_metrics.description: A drawing should be treated as an illustration of the invention and not as confining the invention to the particular angle or dimension shown in the picture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the drawing were the limiting criterion, infringement would require identity with the precise angle or dimension depicted; instead the specification must provide directions enabling construction in other forms, or a skilled workman must be able to do so without difficulty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addressee's assumed skill: no more than ordinary knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee must not, in framing his specification, call upon the persons to whom it is addressed to exercise more than the actual existing knowledge common to their trade or profession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentee may exhaust the common knowledge of the trade but cannot require the addressee to 'tax their ingenuity or invention' or solve problems by exercising the inventive faculty; if he does, the specification is bad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and limits of expert testimony on identity/infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Experts may testify to (1) precise differences or resemblances (matters of fact) and (2) opinions whether those differences are material to substantial identity (matters of opinion), but the boundary between fact and opinion can be shadowy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While experts are admissible to point out resemblances/differences and to opine on materiality, the jury (guided by the court) must exercise judgment; the court should not surrender its function of instructing the jury about the legal significance of those facts (e.g., what constitutes a fresh invention).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity/infringement is a mixed question of law and fact
rubrics_metrics.description: The question whether the thing made or used by the defendant is, in the sense of the patent law, identical with the patentee's invention is the same as the issue on novelty and is a mixed question of law and fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The jury determines observed differences or resemblances (facts), but the court must instruct the jury on what, as a matter of law, constitutes identity or non-identity (e.g., whether changes amount to a fresh invention).

rubrics_metrics.name: Court's duty to instruct on legal significance
rubrics_metrics.description: The duty of giving legal instruction (e.g., whether a particular change amounts, in point of law, to a change of the principle of the machine) should not be surrendered by the court to expert witnesses or the jury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After experts point out differences and express opinions on materiality, the court must instruct the jury whether those differences legally constitute a fresh invention or are merely mechanical/chemical equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissible purposes of skilled witness testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons skilled in the particular subject may (1) point out and explain points of actual resemblance or difference and (2) state, as matter of opinion, whether such resemblances or differences are material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Their opinions on materiality are entitled to respect, but ultimate legal conclusions (fresh invention, identity) remain for the court and jury under legal instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty is a question of fact for the jury (with court guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The question of novelty embraces whether the plaintiff was the inventor and whether the thing patented is substantially different from anything known before; these are facts for the jury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court must instruct the jury on what constitutes novelty in law and what suffices as inventive sufficiency to support a patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior use and notice requirement for defendant
rubrics_metrics.description: When the defendant relies on the fact of a previous invention, knowledge, or use of the thing patented, he must give notice of the names and places of residence of the persons he intends to prove have such prior knowledge or use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive proof of prior existence will outweigh negative evidence offered by the plaintiff; the procedural notice requirement is essential to the defendant's proof strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competency of interested witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons who have used the patented machine are not thereby rendered incompetent as witnesses for interest; patentees who assigned their interest and licensees can be competent witnesses under certain conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although competent, such witnesses' testimony may be given little weight if bias or self-interest is evident; specific case law examples illustrate nuances (e.g., patentee in another patent who sold rights may still be competent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility: when it is fact versus law
rubrics_metrics.description: The question of utility is sometimes a question of fact and sometimes one of law; a 'useful invention' is one not injurious to society, not frivolous or insignificant, and capable of use to derive some advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the invention is clearly injurious or not a patentable subject, utility is a legal question for the court; if the means' practical success is in doubt, utility depends on evidence and is a question of fact for the jury. Degree of usefulness is unimportant, but total failure of an essential claimed part renders the patent invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frivolous or insignificant inventions are for the court
rubrics_metrics.description: If the object proposed is frivolous or insignificant such that no public advantage can be derived, the court should pronounce the patent void as not a patentable subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the object is not clearly frivolous, but the means fail, the matter returns to factual inquiry of usefulness for the jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of the specification and claim extent belongs to the court
rubrics_metrics.description: The construction of the specification as to the extent of the claim is for the court: the court must determine what the claim actually covers and whether the patent is valid in law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The jury takes the court's construction when assessing novelty/validity; if terms of art require explanation by evidence, the jury may be called to find meanings of those terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources for construing a claim: descriptive parts and claim language
rubrics_metrics.description: The court may resort to the descriptive parts of the specification to ascertain what the patentee has said he had invented; if the description is clear, claim language should be construed to include the actual invention previously set forth (ut res magis valeat quam pereat).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The whole specification, including preamble/body/summing-up, should be examined together unless a part explicitly excludes the rest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of extrinsic evidence and evidence of actual invention
rubrics_metrics.description: When the descriptive parts are uncertain, the character and scope of the invention can only be ascertained by attending to evidence: what is new or old, state of the art, and whether a principle had been discovered and applied before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of the inventor's actual contribution, surrounding circumstances, and state of the art will materially affect construction; the judge should 'gather as he goes along' and may give conditional constructions depending on factual findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption against claiming known in-use items
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee is to be presumed not to intend to claim things which he must know to be in use; specifications should be read, consistently with fair import, to make the claim coextensive with the actual discovery or invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The degree to which a thing was known and its familiarity will influence whether the patentee is understood to have claimed it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of general terms in light of the state of the art (ejusdem generis principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: General terms that embrace other substances will be interpreted to include only those substances ejusdem generis with the particular substances mentioned and which may reasonably be supposed, on the state of the art, to have been contemplated at the time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As illustrated by the gas apparatus example, if certain substances were known but not in practical use or too expensive, the patentee's general terms are read to include only those substances reasonably contemplated for use at the patent date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction based on factual statements incorporated into the description
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes construction rests on facts that are referred to as part of the description and govern it; if such facts are controverted they are left to the jury, but if proved or admitted, the court will take notice of them in giving legal construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: where specification described a 'flyer in one continuous piece' and claims summed up combination language, the court considered the admitted facts to determine the kind of flyer intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional versus absolute constructions depending on evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: If facts material to claim construction are not left in doubt by the evidence, the court will give the construction absolutely; if the evidence requires factual findings by the jury, the court will give the construction conditionally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The judge must observe what facts are controverted and what are not, and inform himself by the evidence while determining the legal meaning of the claim.
